analysis.one_liner: Protects workers who report fraud or waste in COVID-19 relief programs from retaliation.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill: it sat in the Homeland Security Committee from June 2020 until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have protected workers at companies, nonprofits, and governments receiving federal COVID-19 relief money from being fired, demoted, or blacklisted for reporting fraud, waste, safety dangers, or abuse of that money. Workers could file retaliation complaints with the Department of Labor within three years, forced-arbitration clauses would not apply to these claims, and pandemic watchdog agencies would run public complaint websites. It died without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at federal contractors, subcontractors, grantees, Paycheck Protection Program recipients, and state or local governments that received COVID relief funds — anyone who reports misuse of that money could not legally be fired, demoted, blacklisted, or threatened for it, and could take the case to the Department of Labor. Taxpayers also benefit indirectly, since fraud in relief programs gets surfaced rather than buried.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at firms getting COVID relief funds

how_it_helps.text: Bars employers receiving federal COVID relief funds from firing, demoting, blacklisting, threatening, or otherwise discriminating against workers who report fraud, gross waste of funds, abuse of authority, dangers to public health or safety, or legal violations in relief programs — and protects workers who are only suspected of reporting.

Lets a worker who faces retaliation file a complaint with the Department of Labor within three years, with the employer required to answer within 60 days; the Labor Secretary can order relief following procedures modeled on the IRS whistleblower rules.

Prevents employers from using predispute arbitration agreements or waivers to strip workers of these rights, keeping retaliation claims in the Labor Department and the courts instead of private arbitration, with a carve-out for union collective bargaining grievances.

Keeps the whistleblower's identity confidential without their written consent, gives them access to the Labor Department's investigative file, and protects them from civil and criminal liability for a protected disclosure; it also requires the pandemic watchdogs to set up public websites for filing complaints.
Appropriates $20 million to the Department of Labor so the complaint system actually has staff and funding behind it.

analysis.who_pays: Employers receiving federal COVID relief money — federal contractors and subcontractors, grantees, PPP recipients, and state or local governments — would face new liability for retaliation, DOL investigations, posting-of-notice requirements, and possible damages. The Treasury would fund the $20 million enforcement appropriation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers receiving federal COVID relief funds

drawbacks.text: Federal employees are excluded — the bill covers only workers of contractors, grantees, relief recipients, and state or local governments, leaving federal workers who witness misuse of relief money to rely on existing, weaker protections.

Employers that received relief funds would face retaliation claims for three years after a worker learns of the alleged reprisal, plus new notice-posting duties, meaning even employers acting in good faith could be dragged into Labor Department proceedings; honest supporters would acknowledge this compliance burden.

The complaint process borrows the IRS whistleblower rules' procedures, adding a layer of adjudication that employers argued (in similar bills) would be slow and hard to navigate for small contractors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — that a nurse, an accountant, or a warehouse worker who sees COVID relief money being stolen can report it without losing their job — is concrete and cheap to deliver relative to the roughly $2 trillion in relief funds it would cover. The costs are real but modest: liability exposure and notice duties for relief recipients and a $20 million appropriation. The bill's biggest design weakness is what it leaves out (federal employees), not what it includes.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2020, referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee, and that committee never held a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Kamala Harris introduced the bill on June 15, 2020 with 10 original cosponsors, during the peak of the pandemic relief spending.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs — the committee that oversees government accountability and contracting.

Thirteen senators (12 Democrats and 1 Independent) cosponsored the bill, but that was the last action ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Contractors, grantees, and other recipients of COVID relief money are better off, because no retaliation-liability regime or public complaint portal was ever created for their programs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: COVID relief recipients, who escaped new liability

for.name: Sen. Kamala Harris
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill with 10 original cosponsors.

against.name: Sen. Ron Johnson
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever scheduled on it.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Controlled the Senate floor and never brought the bill up for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call exists; every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent, and the Republican-run committee and Republican Senate majority took no action on it.

industries.industry: Federal contractors and grantees receiving COVID relief funds
industries.note: The bill would have exposed them to retaliation claims, Labor Department investigations, and damages whenever a worker reports fraud, waste, or safety dangers in relief-funded work. Their interest in avoiding that scrutiny runs against the workers and taxpayers the bill protects.

industries.industry: Paycheck Protection Program recipients and lenders
industries.note: PPP loans are covered funds under the bill, so employees at PPP recipients could have used it to report misuse of loan money without fearing firing. Recipients would have gained a new legal exposure they did not have.

industries.industry: Employment arbitration providers and employers relying on forced arbitration
industries.note: The bill makes predispute arbitration agreements unenforceable for these retaliation claims, moving disputes out of private arbitration into the Labor Department and courts.

industries.industry: State and local governments receiving relief funds
industries.note: Governments and their contractors would count as employers subject to the anti-retaliation rules, notice-posting duties, and complaint procedures. Governments also deliver the relief itself, so the bill's aim of surfacing misuse in their programs serves the public they serve.
